meta.book_title: metricsAI: An Introduction to Econometrics with Python and AI in the Cloud

practice.stem: Practice Exercise 4 gives the log-linear model ln(earnings) = 8.5 + 0.08 × education. Which interpretation of 0.08 is correct?

options.text: Each additional year of education is associated with earnings about $0.08 higher.
options.feedback: The dependent variable is ln(earnings), so the slope describes a proportionate change in earnings, not a change in dollars.

options.text: Each additional year of education is associated with earnings about 8% higher.
options.feedback: Correct. In a log-linear model, 100 × β₂ approximates the percentage change in y for a one-unit increase in x: 100 × 0.08 = 8%.

options.text: A 1% increase in education is associated with earnings about 0.08% higher.
options.feedback: That is how a log-log slope (an elasticity) is read. Here education enters in years, not in logs.

options.text: Each additional year of education is associated with earnings about 0.08% higher.
options.feedback: Multiply the coefficient by 100 to express the change in percent: 0.08 is a proportionate change of 8%.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.1: in ln y = β₁ + β₂x, β₂ is a semi-elasticity, so one more year of education is associated with approximately 100 × 0.08 = 8% higher earnings (exactly, 100(e^0.08 − 1) ≈ 8.3%).

practice.stem: Suppose a wage model gives ln(wage) = 2.1 + 0.25 × union + …, where union = 1 for union members and 0 otherwise. Computed exactly rather than with the 100 × β approximation, union members' predicted wage is higher than that of otherwise similar non-members by about how much?

options.feedback: This is the approximation 100 × 0.25. For a coefficient this large, the approximation and the exact value differ noticeably.
This is 100 × (1 − e^−0.25), the percentage by which non-members fall short of members. The question uses non-members as the base.
This is 100 × e^0.25 without subtracting 1. The exact formula is 100 × (e^β − 1).

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.1: the exact percentage effect of a one-unit change in x is 100(e^β₂ − 1), which matters once |β₂| exceeds about 0.1. Here 100 × (e^0.25 − 1) ≈ 28.4%, compared with the 25% approximation.

practice.stem: Practice Exercise 4 also gives the log-log model ln(earnings) = 3.2 + 0.45 × ln(hours). Which interpretation of 0.45 is correct?

options.text: Earnings are about 0.45% higher for each additional hour worked.
options.feedback: That reading treats hours in levels (a semi-elasticity). Hours enter in logs, so the slope relates percentage changes.

options.text: Earnings are about 45% higher for each additional hour worked.
options.feedback: Hours enter in logs, so the slope refers to a 1% change in hours, and a log-log slope is not multiplied by 100.

options.text: Earnings are about 45% higher when hours are 1% higher.
options.feedback: A log-log slope is already in percent-per-percent terms; it is not multiplied by 100.

options.text: Earnings are about 0.45% higher when hours are 1% higher.
options.feedback: Correct. In a log-log model the slope is an elasticity: the percentage change in y for a 1% change in x.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.1: in ln y = β₁ + β₂ ln x, β₂ is an elasticity. Here a 1% increase in hours is associated with about 0.45% higher earnings, an inelastic relationship (0.45 < 1).

practice.stem: Suppose a log-linear wage model has an experience coefficient of 0.03. For a worker with 10 years of experience and predicted earnings of $40,000, about how many dollars does one more year of experience add to predicted earnings?

options.text: About $1,200
options.feedback: Correct: in a log-linear model ME = β₂ × y, so 0.03 × 40,000 = $1,200.

options.text: About $3
options.feedback: This reads 100 × 0.03 = 3 as dollars. The coefficient is a proportionate change, so it must be multiplied by the earnings level.

options.text: About $12
options.feedback: This treats 0.03 as 0.03% (0.0003 × 40,000 = $12). As a proportion, 0.03 means 3%.

options.text: About $120
options.feedback: This uses the log-log formula β₂ × y / x (0.03 × 40,000 / 10). Experience enters in levels, so ME = β₂ × y.

practice.explanation: Section 15.2: in a log-linear model the dollar marginal effect is ME = β₂ × y, so it grows with the earnings level: 0.03 × $40,000 = $1,200 per year of experience.

practice.stem: Which statements about log transformations are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In a log-linear model, the slope is measured in dollars of y per unit of x.
options.feedback: With ln y as the dependent variable the slope measures a proportionate change in y; 100 × slope is approximately a percentage.

options.text: Logs can turn a multiplicative relationship into a linear one.
options.feedback: Correct: ln(ab) = ln a + ln b, so multiplicative models become additive in logs.

options.text: Logging a right-skewed variable, such as house prices, reduces the influence of its largest values.
options.feedback: Correct: the log compresses large values, which reduces skewness and the pull of outliers.

options.text: Any variable can be logged, including one that equals zero for some observations.
options.feedback: ln(0) is undefined, so observations with zero values would be lost.

options.text: In a log-log model, the slope is an elasticity.
options.feedback: Correct: both variables are in logs, so the slope is a percentage change in y per 1% change in x.

practice.explanation: Section 15.2 lists why logs are common in economics: they linearize multiplicative relationships, give percentage (semi-elasticity or elasticity) interpretations, reduce the influence of outliers, and often make errors more symmetric. They require strictly positive values.

practice.stem: Suppose model A regresses wage on education (R² = 0.20) and model B regresses ln(wage) on education (R² = 0.25). Because 0.25 is larger than 0.20, we can conclude that model B fits wages better.

options.text: True
options.feedback: The two R² values measure fit to different dependent variables (wage versus ln(wage)), so they cannot be compared directly.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Model A's R² measures fit to wages and model B's to ln(wages). To compare them, compare predictions of wages in dollars (for example, their mean squared errors).

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.2: R² is not comparable across models with different dependent variables (y versus ln y). Compare prediction accuracy for y in levels, information criteria, or economic plausibility instead.

practice.stem: Suppose a fitted model is ŷ = 10 − 4x + 0.5x². Which describes its shape?

options.text: An inverted U: y rises, peaks, and then falls as x increases.
options.feedback: An inverted U requires a negative coefficient on x². Here the x² coefficient is +0.5.

options.text: A straight line with slope −4.
options.feedback: The x² term bends the line: the slope is −4 + 2(0.5)x = −4 + x, which changes with x.

options.text: A U shape: y falls, reaches a minimum, and then rises as x increases.
options.feedback: Correct. A positive x² coefficient gives a U shape, with the minimum at x = −(−4)/(2 × 0.5) = 4.

options.text: Falling at every value of x, because the coefficient on x is negative.
options.feedback: The slope −4 + x is negative only for x < 4; beyond x = 4 the curve rises.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.3: in y = β₁ + β₂x + β₃x², β₃ > 0 gives a U shape and β₃ < 0 an inverted U. Here the turning point is x* = −β₂/(2β₃) = 4/1 = 4, a minimum.

practice.stem: For the fitted model ŷ = 2 + 3x + 4x² in Practice Exercise 1, at what value of x is the turning point?

options.feedback: Correct: x* = −β₂/(2β₃) = −3/(2 × 4) = −0.375. Since β₃ > 0, this is a minimum.
This is −β₂/β₃ = −3/4, without the 2 in the denominator.
Check the sign: x* = −β₂/(2β₃) with β₂ = 3 and β₃ = 4 is negative.
This is −3/16, which divides by 4β₃ instead of 2β₃.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.3: the turning point is where ME = β₂ + 2β₃x = 0, so x* = −β₂/(2β₃) = −3/8 = −0.375. With β₃ = 4 > 0 the curve is U-shaped and this is its minimum.

practice.stem: For the same model ŷ = 2 + 3x + 4x², what is the marginal effect of x at x = 2?

options.feedback: This is 3 + 4 × 2, which drops the factor 2 from the derivative of 4x².
Correct: ME = β₂ + 2β₃x = 3 + 2 × 4 × 2 = 19.
This is the coefficient on x alone. With an x² term, the marginal effect depends on x.
This is 2β₃x = 16 alone, which leaves out β₂ = 3.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.3: ME = ∂ŷ/∂x = β₂ + 2β₃x = 3 + 8x, so at x = 2 the marginal effect is 3 + 16 = 19.

practice.stem: For ŷ = 2 + 3x + 4x², the marginal effect of x at x = 3 is larger than the marginal effect at x = 1.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. ME = 3 + 8x is 27 at x = 3 and 11 at x = 1: with β₃ > 0, the slope grows with x.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Compute ME = β₂ + 2β₃x at both values of x (Key Concept 15.3).

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.3: in a quadratic model the marginal effect β₂ + 2β₃x varies with x. Here it is 11 at x = 1 and 27 at x = 3.

practice.concept: AME, MEM, and MER (Key Concepts glossary, Section 15.3)
practice.stem: A study reports the marginal effect of experience on wages separately for workers with 5, 15, and 25 years of experience. Which type of marginal effect is this?

options.text: Average marginal effect (AME)
options.feedback: The AME is a single summary number; this study reports three separate effects at chosen experience levels.

options.text: Marginal effect at representative values (MER)
options.feedback: Correct. Evaluating the marginal effect at chosen, policy-relevant values of the regressor gives MERs.

options.text: Marginal effect at the mean (MEM)
options.feedback: The MEM is a single number; this study reports three separate effects at chosen experience levels.

options.text: Standardized coefficient
options.feedback: A standardized coefficient rescales a slope into standard-deviation units; it is not evaluated at chosen values of x.

practice.explanation: Key Concepts glossary: MER plugs chosen values of the regressors (here 5, 15, and 25 years of experience) into the marginal-effect formula, giving several effects, each tailored to a profile of interest.

practice.concept: AME, MEM, and MER (Key Concepts glossary, Section 15.3)
practice.stem: Suppose ŷ = 2 + 3x + 4x² and the data contain the values x = 1, 2, and 3. The average marginal effect (AME) of x equals 3, the coefficient on x.

options.text: True
options.feedback: The AME averages the marginal effect over the observations. With an x² term, the marginal effect is not the coefficient on x.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The marginal effects 3 + 8x are 11, 19, and 27 at x = 1, 2, and 3, so the AME is (11 + 19 + 27)/3 = 19, not 3.

practice.explanation: Key Concepts glossary (AME) and Practice Exercise 1(b): compute the marginal effect for each observation and average: (11 + 19 + 27)/3 = 19. The coefficient 3 would be the marginal effect only at x = 0.

practice.stem: Suppose a researcher with only 20 observations adds x³, x⁴, and x⁵ to a quadratic model in x. What is the main risk?

options.text: OLS can no longer be used to estimate the model.
options.feedback: Adding powers of x does not stop OLS from estimating the model; the concern lies elsewhere (see the Polynomial Regression glossary entry).

options.text: The coefficients turn into elasticities.
options.feedback: Elasticities come from log-log models. Powers of x do not change what is logged.

options.text: The marginal effect of x becomes constant.
options.feedback: Higher powers make the marginal effect vary even more with x, not less.

options.text: Overfitting: the extra bends chase noise in a small sample.
options.feedback: Correct. Each extra power adds a bend; with 20 observations the curve can fit noise rather than the true relationship.

practice.explanation: Key Concepts glossary (Polynomial Regression): cubic and higher terms add bends but invite overfitting in small samples. The quadratic is the most common choice.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of test scores on study hours and hours² gives t = 1.6 for hours and t = −1.4 for hours², while the joint F-test that both coefficients are zero has p = 0.001. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Judged by the joint test, study hours are related to test scores.
options.feedback: Correct: the joint test of both terms (p = 0.001) asks whether study hours matter at all, in any functional form.

options.text: Since neither t-statistic exceeds 1.96, study hours can be dropped from the model.
options.feedback: Individual t-tests can mislead when hours and hours² are highly correlated. The joint test rejects strongly.

options.text: Modest individual t-statistics are expected here, since hours and hours² move almost in lockstep.
options.feedback: Correct: when two regressors are nearly collinear, the data cannot separate their effects well, so each coefficient is imprecise even though together they matter.

options.text: The joint test shows that the turning point is statistically significant.
options.feedback: The joint test asks whether both coefficients are zero; it does not test the location of the turning point.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.4: test x and x² jointly with an F-test. Individual t-tests can be small because x and x² are highly correlated, even when the variable clearly matters.

practice.stem: In Practice Exercise 5, education has coefficient 3,000 and standard deviation s<sub>x</sub> = 3, and the standard deviation of earnings is s<sub>y</sub> = 25,000. What is education's standardized coefficient?

options.feedback: This is 3,000/25,000, which leaves out s<sub>x</sub>.
This uses the variance of education (3² = 9) instead of its standard deviation.
Correct: β* = β × s<sub>x</sub>/s<sub>y</sub> = 3,000 × 3 / 25,000 = 0.36.
This is 3,000 × 3, the dollar change for a one-SD change in education; dividing by s<sub>y</sub> = 25,000 expresses it in SDs of earnings.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.5: β* = β × (s<sub>x</sub>/s<sub>y</sub>) = 3,000 × 3 / 25,000 = 0.36: a one-SD increase in education (3 years) is associated with a 0.36-SD increase in earnings.

practice.stem: Suppose a regression of test scores on class size and other regressors gives a standardized coefficient of −0.15 for class size. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Test scores are about 0.15 standard deviations lower when class size is one standard deviation larger, other regressors fixed.
options.feedback: Correct. A standardized coefficient measures both x and y in standard deviations.

options.text: Class size explains about 15% of the variation in test scores.
options.feedback: A standardized coefficient is a slope in SD units, not a share of explained variation (that would be an R²-type measure).

options.text: Test scores are about 0.15 standard deviations lower for each additional student per class, other regressors fixed.
options.feedback: In a standardized coefficient, x is also measured in standard deviations, not in its natural units.

options.text: Test scores are about 0.15 points lower when class size is one standard deviation larger, other regressors fixed.
options.feedback: In a standardized coefficient, y is also measured in standard deviations, not in its natural units.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.5: β* is the change in y, in SDs of y, associated with a one-SD increase in x. Here, a one-SD larger class is associated with test scores 0.15 SD lower.

practice.stem: In Practice Exercise 5 (s<sub>y</sub> = 25,000), age has coefficient 500 and s<sub>x</sub> = 10, education has coefficient 3,000 and s<sub>x</sub> = 3, and hours have coefficient 200 and s<sub>x</sub> = 8. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Education has the largest standardized coefficient of the three.
options.feedback: Correct: 3,000 × 3/25,000 = 0.36, versus 0.20 for age and 0.064 for hours.

options.text: Age has a larger standardized coefficient than hours.
options.feedback: Correct: 500 × 10/25,000 = 0.20 for age, versus 200 × 8/25,000 = 0.064 for hours.

options.text: Since age's raw coefficient is 2.5 times that of hours, its standardized coefficient is also 2.5 times as large.
options.feedback: The ratio also depends on the standard deviations: 0.20/0.064 ≈ 3.1, not 2.5.

options.text: Each standardized coefficient can be computed from the raw coefficient and the standard deviations of x and y, without re-estimating the model.
options.feedback: Correct: β* = β × s<sub>x</sub>/s<sub>y</sub> uses only the raw coefficient and two standard deviations.

options.text: Education's standardized coefficient is the share of earnings variation that education explains.
options.feedback: A standardized coefficient is a slope in SD units, not a share of explained variation.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.5: β*(age) = 0.20, β*(education) = 0.36, β*(hours) = 0.064, so education ranks first, then age, then hours. Raw coefficients cannot be ranked directly because the regressors have different units and spreads.

practice.stem: For the fitted model ŷ = 1 + 2x + 4d + 7(d × x) in Practice Exercise 2, what is the marginal effect of x when d = 1?

options.feedback: Correct: ME<sub>x</sub> = β₂ + β₄d = 2 + 7 × 1 = 9.
This is the marginal effect of x when d = 0. With the interaction, the effect of x depends on d.
This is the interaction coefficient alone, which is the difference between the slopes for d = 1 and d = 0.
This adds the coefficient on d (4). The d coefficient shifts the level, not the slope in x.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.6: with an interaction, ME<sub>x</sub> = β₂ + β₄d = 2 + 7d, so the slope in x is 2 when d = 0 and 9 when d = 1.

practice.stem: Suppose a wage model includes experience, a female dummy, and their interaction, and the interaction coefficient is insignificant (p = 0.45). Which step does the chapter recommend?

options.text: Drop experience as well, since its interaction with female is insignificant.
options.feedback: The chapter warns against dropping a main effect because an interaction is insignificant.

options.text: Report the interaction coefficient alone as the return to experience.
options.feedback: The interaction is the difference in slopes between groups; the return to experience also involves the main effect.

options.text: Keep the main effects and judge each variable with a joint test of its main effect and interaction.
options.feedback: Correct. Individual t-tests are unreliable here; the chapter advises joint F-tests and keeping the main effects.

options.text: Judge whether gender matters from the t-test on the female coefficient alone.
options.feedback: With an interaction, the female coefficient is the gender gap only at zero experience; the chapter advises a joint test of the dummy and its interaction.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.6 and Section 15.5 ('Practical Advice'): test interactions jointly with their main effects, and keep the main effects even when an interaction is insignificant.

practice.stem: In ŷ = 1 + 2x + 4d + 7(d × x), the coefficient 2 is the marginal effect of x for observations with d = 0.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. ME<sub>x</sub> = 2 + 7d, which equals 2 when d = 0.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Write out ME<sub>x</sub> = β₂ + β₄d and evaluate it at d = 0 (Key Concept 15.6).

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.6: in a model with x × d, the coefficient on x is the marginal effect of x when d = 0; for d = 1 it is 2 + 7 = 9.

practice.stem: For the same model ŷ = 1 + 2x + 4d + 7(d × x), what is the marginal effect of d (the change in ŷ when d goes from 0 to 1) at x = 3?

options.feedback: This is the coefficient on d alone, which is the effect of d only at x = 0.
This is 4 + 7, which forgets to multiply the interaction coefficient by x = 3.
This is 7 × 3, which leaves out the coefficient on d.
Correct: ME<sub>d</sub> = β₃ + β₄x = 4 + 7 × 3 = 25.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.6 (applied to d): ME<sub>d</sub> = β₃ + β₄x = 4 + 7x, which is 25 at x = 3.

practice.stem: Suppose an insurer models ln(annual medical cost) and predicts each patient's cost as exp(predicted ln cost). On average, how do these naive predictions compare with actual costs?

options.text: They overpredict, because exponentiating exaggerates large values.
options.feedback: The naive predictions are systematically too low, not too high (Key Concept 15.7).

options.text: They underpredict, so a correction factor above 1 is needed.
options.feedback: Correct. Naive retransformation systematically underestimates E[y|x]; multiplying by a factor above 1 corrects it.

options.text: They are unbiased, because the log-model residuals average zero.
options.feedback: The residuals average zero on the log scale, but that property does not carry over to exp of the predictions; see Key Concept 15.7.

options.text: They are unbiased once the sample is large enough.
options.feedback: The bias comes from converting log predictions back to levels, so a larger sample does not remove it.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.7: exp(predicted ln y) systematically underestimates E[y|x], so predictions in levels need a correction factor (the chapter's healthcare example: a naive $8,000 versus an adjusted $10,000).

practice.stem: For the model predicted ln y = 1 + 2x with s<sub>e</sub> = 0.3 (Practice Exercise 3), what is the bias-corrected prediction of y at x = 1, using the normal correction factor?

options.feedback: This is the naive prediction e³. It needs the correction factor exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2).
This multiplies by exp(s<sub>e</sub>²) = exp(0.09); the factor is exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2).
This multiplies by exp(s<sub>e</sub>/2) = exp(0.15); s<sub>e</sub> must be squared.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.7: under normal homoskedastic errors, ỹ = exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2) × exp(predicted ln y). At x = 1 the predicted log is 3, so ỹ = e³ × e^0.045 ≈ 21.01, about 4.6% above the naive 20.09.

practice.stem: Duan's smearing estimator multiplies the naive prediction exp(predicted ln y) by exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2).

options.text: True
options.feedback: exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2) is the normality-based factor. The smearing estimator multiplies by a different, residual-based quantity.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. Smearing multiplies by (1/n)Σexp(ûᵢ), the average of the exponentiated residuals, not by exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2).

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.7: the normality-based correction multiplies by exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2); Duan's smearing estimator multiplies by (1/n)Σexp(ûᵢ), computed from the residuals themselves.

practice.stem: Suppose a hospital models ln(cost) with s<sub>e</sub> = 0.8 and adds up exp(predicted ln cost) over 10,000 patients to forecast total cost. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The correction should also be applied to the coefficients before reading them as percentage effects.
options.feedback: The correction is for predictions in levels; coefficient interpretation in the log model needs no adjustment.

options.text: The naive total is likely to understate expected total cost.
options.feedback: Correct: each naive prediction is too low on average, so their sum is too low as well.

options.text: Dividing the naive predictions by 1.38 would remove the bias.
options.feedback: The naive predictions are too low, so they must be multiplied, not divided, by the correction factor.

options.text: The normal-based factor exp(0.8²/2) = exp(0.32) ≈ 1.38 raises each naive prediction by about 38%.
options.feedback: Correct: exp(0.32) ≈ 1.377, so each prediction is multiplied by about 1.38.

options.text: A larger s<sub>e</sub> would make the naive forecast more accurate.
options.feedback: A larger s<sub>e</sub> means a larger correction factor, so the naive forecast falls further short.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.7: naive predictions understate expected cost, and the shortfall adds up over many patients. With s<sub>e</sub> = 0.8 the normal-based factor is exp(0.32) ≈ 1.38.

practice.concept: Models with mixed regressor types (Section 15.7, Key Concept 15.8)
practice.stem: Suppose a wage model is ln(wage) = … − 0.12 × rural + …, where rural = 1 for rural workers, and the model also controls for education and experience. Which interpretation of −0.12 is correct?

options.text: Rural workers earn approximately $0.12 less per hour than comparable urban workers.
options.feedback: The dependent variable is ln(wage), so the coefficient is a proportionate difference, not dollars.

options.text: Rural workers earn approximately 0.12% less than comparable urban workers.
options.feedback: Multiply by 100: a coefficient of −0.12 is a proportionate difference of about 12%.

options.text: Rural workers earn approximately 12% less than urban workers with the same education and experience.
options.feedback: Correct. A dummy in a log-linear model gives an approximate percentage difference, holding the other regressors fixed (exactly, 100(e^−0.12 − 1) ≈ −11.3%).

options.text: Rural workers earn approximately 12% less than urban workers, before accounting for education and experience.
options.feedback: The coefficient compares workers with the same education and experience; the raw gap may be larger or smaller.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.8: dummies are interpreted as group differences; with ln(wage) as the dependent variable, 100 × β approximates the percentage difference holding the other regressors fixed (here about −12%; exactly about −11.3%).

practice.concept: Models with mixed regressor types (Section 15.7, Key Concept 15.8)
practice.stem: Suppose a production function is estimated as ln(output) = 1.1 + 0.6 × ln(labor) + …. If labor rises by 5%, other inputs fixed, output changes by approximately how much?

options.text: About 3%
options.feedback: Correct: with elasticity 0.6, a 5% increase in labor is associated with about 0.6 × 5 = 3% more output.

options.text: About 0.6%
options.feedback: 0.6% is the change for a 1% increase in labor; here labor rises by 5%.

options.text: About 60%
options.feedback: This multiplies the elasticity by 100. A log-log slope is already in percent-per-percent terms.

options.text: About 8.3%
options.feedback: This divides 5 by 0.6. The elasticity multiplies the percentage change in x.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.1: in a log-log model, %Δy ≈ β₂ × %Δx = 0.6 × 5 = 3%.

practice.concept: Models with mixed regressor types (Section 15.7, Key Concept 15.8)
practice.stem: Suppose ln(wage) = 1.5 + 0.04 × exper − 0.0005 × exper² + …. For a worker with 10 years of experience, one more year of experience is associated with a wage approximately how much higher?

options.feedback: This uses the coefficient on exper alone. With exper², the effect depends on experience.
This is 0.04 − 0.0005 × 10, which drops the factor 2 from the derivative of exper².
The marginal effect 0.03 is a proportionate change; multiply by 100 to express it in percent.

practice.explanation: Key Concepts 15.3 and 15.8: with ln(wage) and a quadratic in experience, the approximate percentage effect is 100 × (β₂ + 2β₃ × exper) = 100 × (0.04 − 0.01) = 3.0% at 10 years.

practice.concept: Models with mixed regressor types (Section 15.7, Key Concept 15.8)
practice.stem: Suppose ln(sales) = … + 0.40 × ln(advertising spending) + 0.03 × years in business + …. The fact that 0.40 is larger than 0.03 does not by itself show that advertising matters more for sales than years in business.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. 0.40 is an elasticity (per 1% more advertising) and 0.03 a semi-elasticity (per extra year in business); they measure different units of change.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Ask what change in advertising and what change in years in business each coefficient refers to (Key Concepts 15.1 and 15.8).

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.8: each coefficient is read according to its transformation. Comparing raw coefficients across different units says nothing about relative importance; standardized coefficients (Section 15.4) are designed for that.

practice.concept: Models with mixed regressor types (Section 15.7, Key Concept 15.8)
practice.stem: Suppose ln(price) = β₁ + β₂ ln(size) + β₃ bedrooms + β₄ age + β₅ age² + β₆ pool + u, where pool = 1 if the house has a pool. Which interpretations are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: β₂ is the elasticity of price with respect to size.
options.feedback: Correct: both price and size are in logs.

options.text: β₄ alone gives the percentage effect of one more year of house age at every age.
options.feedback: Age enters as a quadratic, so the effect is 100 × (β₄ + 2β₅ × age), which varies with age.

options.text: 100 × β₆ approximates the percentage price difference between otherwise similar houses with and without a pool.
options.feedback: Correct: a dummy in a log-linear model gives an approximate percentage difference.

options.text: 100 × β₃ approximates the percentage change in price for one more bedroom, other regressors fixed.
options.feedback: Correct: bedrooms enter in levels and price in logs, a semi-elasticity.

practice.explanation: Key Concept 15.8: in one model, a logged regressor gives an elasticity, a level regressor a semi-elasticity, a dummy an approximate percentage difference, and a quadratic a marginal effect that varies with the regressor.

exam.stem: For the 872 workers, the chapter's log-linear model is ln(earnings) = 8.962 + 0.0078 × age + 0.1006 × education. Which interpretation of 0.1006 is correct?

options.text: Holding age fixed, one more year of education is associated with earnings about $0.10 higher.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a log-linear model is interpreted (Section 15.2, Key Concept 15.1).

options.text: Holding age fixed, a 1% increase in education is associated with earnings about 0.10% higher.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a log-linear model is interpreted (Section 15.2, Key Concept 15.1).

options.text: Holding age fixed, one more year of education is associated with earnings about 10.1% higher.
options.feedback: Correct. In a log-linear model, 100 × β approximates the percentage change in y for a one-unit increase in x.

options.text: Holding age fixed, one more year of education is associated with earnings about 0.10% higher.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a log-linear model is interpreted (Section 15.2, Key Concept 15.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.1: the education coefficient is a semi-elasticity, so one more year of schooling is associated with approximately 100 × 0.1006 ≈ 10.1% higher earnings (exactly, 100(e^0.1006 − 1) ≈ 10.6%), close to the classic Mincer return of about 10%.

exam.stem: In the same log-linear model, two workers of the same age differ by four years of education, so predicted ln(earnings) differs by 4 × 0.1006 = 0.4024. Using the exact formula, by about what percentage are the more-educated worker's predicted earnings higher?

options.feedback: Revisit the exact formula for percentage changes in Key Concept 15.1.
Revisit the exact formula for percentage changes in Key Concept 15.1.
Revisit the exact formula for percentage changes in Key Concept 15.1.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.1: the exact change is 100 × (e^Δln y − 1) = 100 × (e^0.4024 − 1) ≈ 49.5%. The approximation 100 × 0.4024 ≈ 40.2% understates it, and one-year exact effects compound rather than add (4 × 10.6% ≈ 42.3% is also too low).

exam.stem: The chapter's log-log model is ln(earnings) = 8.009 + 0.346 × ln(age) + 0.1004 × education. Which interpretation of 0.346 is correct?

options.text: Holding education fixed, a 1% increase in age is associated with earnings about 0.35% higher.
options.feedback: Correct. In a log-log model the slope is an elasticity: the percentage change in y for a 1% change in x.

options.text: Holding education fixed, one more year of age is associated with earnings about 0.35% higher.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a log-log model is interpreted (Section 15.2, Key Concept 15.1).

options.text: Holding education fixed, one more year of age is associated with earnings about 34.6% higher.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a log-log model is interpreted (Section 15.2, Key Concept 15.1).

options.text: Holding education fixed, a 1% increase in age is associated with earnings about 34.6% higher.
options.feedback: Revisit how the slope of a log-log model is interpreted (Section 15.2, Key Concept 15.1).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.1: in ln y = β₁ + β₂ ln x, β₂ is an elasticity. A 1% increase in age (about 0.4 years at age 40) is associated with about 0.35% higher earnings, an inelastic relationship.

exam.stem: In the chapter's log-linear model, the age coefficient is 0.0078. Suppose a 40-year-old worker's predicted earnings are $60,000. About how many dollars does one more year of age add to predicted earnings, holding education fixed?

options.text: About $0.78
options.feedback: Revisit the marginal-effect formulas for log models in Section 15.2.

options.text: About $4.68
options.feedback: Revisit the marginal-effect formulas for log models in Section 15.2.

options.text: About $12
options.feedback: Revisit the marginal-effect formulas for log models in Section 15.2.

options.text: About $468
options.feedback: Correct: in a log-linear model ME = β × y = 0.0078 × 60,000 ≈ $468.

exam.explanation: Section 15.2: in a log-linear model ME<sub>x</sub> = β₂ × y, so the dollar effect of a year of age grows with the earnings level: 0.0078 × $60,000 ≈ $468 (about 0.78% of $60,000).

exam.stem: Which of the following are reasons the chapter gives for modeling ln(earnings) rather than earnings? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Earnings are right-skewed: the sample mean ($56,369) is well above the median ($44,200).
options.feedback: Correct: a long upper tail is a standard reason to model the log of earnings.

options.text: Economic theory often suggests multiplicative relationships, which become linear in logs.
options.feedback: Correct: logs turn multiplicative relationships into additive ones.

options.text: Logs can be taken of zero earnings, so no worker is dropped from the sample.
options.feedback: Revisit the reasons for using logarithmic transformations listed in Section 15.2.

options.text: Logging earnings often reduces heteroskedasticity.
options.feedback: Correct: the chapter lists this among the reasons to choose a log model.

options.text: With ln(earnings) as the dependent variable, each coefficient is read directly as a dollar change in earnings.
options.feedback: Revisit the reasons for using logarithmic transformations listed in Section 15.2.

exam.explanation: Section 15.2: logs linearize multiplicative relationships, reduce the influence of outliers and skewness (here the mean of $56,369 exceeds the median of $44,200), often reduce heteroskedasticity, and give percentage interpretations. The log of zero is undefined (every worker in this sample earns at least $4,000).

exam.stem: The chapter's log-linear model has a higher R² (0.190) than its levels model with the same regressors (0.115), but this comparison alone does not show that the log-linear model fits earnings better.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. One R² measures fit to ln(earnings) and the other to earnings, so the two numbers are on different scales.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit what each R² measures when the dependent variables differ (Key Concept 15.2).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.2: R² cannot be compared across models with different dependent variables (y versus ln y). Compare predictions of earnings in dollars (for example, mean squared errors), information criteria, or economic plausibility instead.

exam.stem: In the chapter's quadratic model, earnings = −98,620 + 3,105 × age − 29.66 × age² + 5,740 × education. Holding education fixed, which describes the shape of predicted earnings against age?

options.text: A U shape: predicted earnings fall with age at first and then rise.
options.feedback: Revisit how the signs of the coefficients determine the shape of a quadratic model (Key Concept 15.3).

options.text: An inverted U: predicted earnings rise with age, peak, and then decline.
options.feedback: Correct. A negative coefficient on age² bends the curve downward, giving an inverted U.

options.text: Predicted earnings rise with age at an increasing rate.
options.feedback: Revisit how the signs of the coefficients determine the shape of a quadratic model (Key Concept 15.3).

options.text: A straight line with a slope of $3,105 per year of age.
options.feedback: Revisit how the signs of the coefficients determine the shape of a quadratic model (Key Concept 15.3).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.3: with β₃ < 0 the quadratic is an inverted U. With β₂ > 0 and β₃ < 0, earnings rise with age, peak at the turning point, and then decline — the classic life-cycle profile.

exam.stem: Using the same quadratic model (age coefficient 3,105, age² coefficient −29.66), at about what age is the turning point of the age–earnings profile, holding education fixed?

options.text: About 26.2 years
options.feedback: Revisit the turning-point formula in Key Concept 15.3.

options.text: About 104.7 years
options.feedback: Revisit the turning-point formula in Key Concept 15.3.

options.text: About 43.3 years
options.feedback: Revisit the turning-point formula in Key Concept 15.3.

options.text: About 52.3 years

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.3: the turning point is where the marginal effect is zero: age* = −β₂/(2β₃) = 3,105/59.32 ≈ 52.3 years, inside the sample's 25–65 age range.

exam.stem: In the same quadratic model, what is the marginal effect of age on predicted earnings for a 40-year-old, holding education fixed?

options.text: $3,105 per year of age
options.feedback: Revisit how the marginal effect of a regressor is computed in a quadratic model (Key Concept 15.3).

options.text: $1,919 per year of age
options.feedback: Revisit how the marginal effect of a regressor is computed in a quadratic model (Key Concept 15.3).

options.text: −$2,373 per year of age
options.feedback: Revisit how the marginal effect of a regressor is computed in a quadratic model (Key Concept 15.3).

options.text: $732 per year of age

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.3: ME<sub>age</sub> = β₂ + 2β₃ × age = 3,105 − 59.32 × 40 ≈ $732 per year at age 40, much smaller than at age 25 (about $1,622) and negative beyond the peak.

exam.stem: In the chapter's quadratic model, predicted earnings keep rising with age all the way to age 65, only more and more slowly.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the turning point of a quadratic model and the shape of the chapter's age–earnings profile (Section 15.3).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. The marginal effect of age turns negative after the turning point (about 52 years), so predicted earnings decline between about 52 and 65.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.3 and Section 15.3: the turning point is about 52.3 years, inside the 25–65 range, so predicted earnings fall for older workers (the marginal effect is about −$454 at age 60).

exam.concept: AME, MEM, and MER (Key Concepts glossary, Section 15.3)
exam.stem: Which description defines the marginal effect at the mean (MEM)?

options.text: The average of the marginal effects computed for each observation in the sample
options.feedback: Revisit the glossary entries for AME, MEM, and MER (Key Concepts).

options.text: The marginal effect evaluated at chosen profiles, such as ages 25, 40, and 55
options.feedback: Revisit the glossary entries for AME, MEM, and MER (Key Concepts).

options.text: The marginal effect evaluated at the sample means of the regressors
options.feedback: Correct. The MEM plugs the sample means of the regressors into the marginal-effect formula.

options.text: The coefficient on x in a model that leaves out x²
options.feedback: Revisit the glossary entries for AME, MEM, and MER (Key Concepts).

exam.explanation: Key Concepts glossary: the AME averages the observation-level marginal effects; the MEM evaluates the marginal effect at the sample means; the MER evaluates it at chosen representative values.

exam.concept: AME, MEM, and MER (Key Concepts glossary, Section 15.3)
exam.stem: In the chapter's quadratic earnings model, the AME of age and the MEM of age are equal.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. The marginal effect β₂ + 2β₃ × age is linear in age, so averaging it over the workers gives the same value as evaluating it at the mean age (about $536).

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the glossary entries for AME and MEM, and how the marginal effect depends on age in a quadratic model.

exam.explanation: Key Concepts glossary (MEM): in a quadratic model the marginal effect is linear in x, so the average of β₂ + 2β₃xᵢ equals β₂ + 2β₃x̄. Here both are about $536. The two diverge only when the marginal effect is itself nonlinear in x.

exam.stem: Which statement about estimating the chapter's quadratic model earnings = β₁ + β₂ age + β₃ age² + β₄ education + u is correct?

options.text: It requires nonlinear least squares, because earnings are a nonlinear function of age.
options.feedback: Revisit how polynomial regression models are estimated (Section 15.3).

options.text: OLS applies, because the model is linear in the coefficients; age² is one more regressor.
options.feedback: Correct. Polynomial regression captures curvature while staying linear in the parameters, so OLS applies.

options.text: OLS applies once age is standardized, because age and age² have different units.
options.feedback: Revisit how polynomial regression models are estimated (Section 15.3).

options.text: OLS applies provided the turning point lies inside the sample's range of ages.
options.feedback: Revisit how polynomial regression models are estimated (Section 15.3).

exam.explanation: Section 15.3: polynomial regression allows nonlinear relationships while maintaining linearity in parameters. The squared term is just another regressor, so the model is estimated by OLS.

exam.stem: In the chapter's quadratic model, age has t = 2.86 and age² has t = −2.38, the correlation between age and age² is 0.99, and the joint F-test of H₀: β<sub>age</sub> = 0 and β<sub>agesq</sub> = 0 gives F = 18.6 with p < 0.001. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The joint F-test, not the t-test on age² alone, answers whether age matters for earnings at all.
options.feedback: Correct: age enters through two terms, so whether it matters is a joint question about both coefficients.

options.text: Because age and age² are correlated at 0.99, age² should be dropped and the model re-estimated with age alone.
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 15.4 on how to decide whether the quadratic term belongs in the model.

options.text: A correlation of 0.99 between two regressors means that OLS cannot estimate the model.
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 15.4 and the multicollinearity discussion in Section 15.5.

options.text: The high correlation between age and age² tends to inflate the standard errors of their individual coefficients.
options.feedback: Correct: highly correlated regressors make individual coefficients imprecise, so individual t-statistics understate the joint evidence.

options.text: The significant joint test shows that the quadratic model fits earnings better than the log-linear model.
options.feedback: Revisit Key Concept 15.2 on comparing models with different dependent variables.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.4: test x and x² jointly. Age and age² are almost perfectly correlated (0.99), which inflates individual standard errors; the joint test (F ≈ 18.6, p < 0.001) shows that age matters. A joint test within one model says nothing about a model with a different dependent variable.

exam.stem: In the chapter's levels model with mixed regressors, the education coefficient is 5,399. Education has standard deviation 2.884 years, and earnings have standard deviation $51,516. What is education's standardized coefficient?

options.feedback: Revisit the formula for standardized coefficients in Key Concept 15.5.
Revisit the formula for standardized coefficients in Key Concept 15.5.
Revisit the formula for standardized coefficients in Key Concept 15.5.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.5: β* = β × (s<sub>x</sub>/s<sub>y</sub>) = 5,399 × 2.884 / 51,516 ≈ 0.30. A one-SD increase in education (about 2.9 years) is associated with earnings about 0.30 SD higher, holding the other regressors fixed.

exam.stem: In the same model, the standardized coefficient on ln(hours) is 0.22. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Earnings are about 0.22 standard deviations higher when ln(hours) is one standard deviation higher, other regressors fixed.
options.feedback: Correct. Both the regressor and earnings are measured in standard deviations.

options.text: Earnings are about $0.22 higher when ln(hours) is one standard deviation higher, other regressors fixed.
options.feedback: Revisit how a standardized coefficient is interpreted (Key Concept 15.5).

options.text: Hours worked explain about 22% of the variation in earnings, other regressors fixed.
options.feedback: Revisit how a standardized coefficient is interpreted (Key Concept 15.5).

options.text: Earnings are about 0.22 standard deviations higher for each additional hour worked per week, other regressors fixed.
options.feedback: Revisit how a standardized coefficient is interpreted (Key Concept 15.5).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.5: β* = 0.22 means a one-SD increase in ln(hours) is associated with a 0.22-SD increase in earnings (about 0.22 × $51,516 ≈ $11,300), holding the other regressors fixed.

exam.stem: In the same levels model, the standardized coefficients of the other regressors are 0.68 (age), −0.57 (age²), 0.22 (ln hours), −0.14 (gender, 1 = female), 0.05 (self-employed), and −0.002 (government). Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The gender value means that women earn about 14% less than men, holding the other regressors fixed.
options.feedback: Revisit how a standardized coefficient is interpreted (Key Concept 15.5).

options.text: The government value indicates essentially no association with earnings once the other regressors are held fixed.
options.feedback: Correct: −0.002 standard deviations is essentially zero.

options.text: A regressor's standardized coefficient depends on how much that regressor varies in the sample.
options.feedback: Correct: β* = β × s<sub>x</sub>/s<sub>y</sub>, so a regressor with little sample variation gets a small β*.

options.text: Standardized coefficients are preferable to raw coefficients for cost–benefit policy analysis.
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's list of when standardized coefficients are and are not useful (Section 15.4).

exam.explanation: Section 15.4: standardized coefficients compare regressors on a common SD scale; they depend on sample variation and are not suited to policy analysis, which needs actual units. Gender's −0.14 is in SDs of earnings, not a percentage; the government dummy's −0.002 is essentially zero.

exam.stem: The chapter's interaction model is earnings = −29,089 + 127 × age + 4,515 × education + 29.04 × (age × education). What is the marginal effect of one more year of education for a 50-year-old?

options.text: $4,515 per year of education
options.feedback: Revisit how the marginal effect of a regressor is computed when it is interacted with another (Key Concept 15.6).

options.text: $1,452 per year of education
options.feedback: Revisit how the marginal effect of a regressor is computed when it is interacted with another (Key Concept 15.6).

options.text: $5,967 per year of education
options.feedback: Correct: ME<sub>education</sub> = 4,515 + 29.04 × 50 ≈ $5,967.

options.text: $4,544 per year of education
options.feedback: Revisit how the marginal effect of a regressor is computed when it is interacted with another (Key Concept 15.6).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.6: ME<sub>education</sub> = β<sub>education</sub> + β<sub>interaction</sub> × age = 4,515 + 29.04 × 50 ≈ $5,967 at age 50.

exam.stem: In the interaction model, the coefficient on age × education is 29.04 with a robust standard error of 56.05 (t = 0.52, p = 0.60). Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The return to education reliably rises with age, by about $29 per extra year of age.
options.feedback: Revisit what an insignificant coefficient does and does not show (Section 15.5).

options.text: Education is unrelated to earnings, because its interaction with age is insignificant.
options.feedback: Revisit what an insignificant coefficient does and does not show (Section 15.5).

options.text: The data give no reliable evidence that the return to education changes with age.
options.feedback: Correct. With p = 0.60, the small positive interaction is well within sampling noise.

options.text: The data show that the return to education is the same at every age.
options.feedback: Revisit what an insignificant coefficient does and does not show (Section 15.5).

exam.explanation: Section 15.5: the interaction is small and statistically insignificant (t ≈ 0.52, p ≈ 0.60), so there is no reliable evidence that education's return varies with age. Failing to reject does not prove the interaction is zero, and it says nothing against education's overall association with earnings.

exam.stem: In the interaction model, the education coefficient (4,515) is the marginal effect of education for a worker of average age.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Revisit the chapter's advice on interpreting main-effect coefficients in interaction models (Section 15.5, 'Practical Advice').

options.text: False
options.feedback: Correct. ME<sub>education</sub> = 4,515 + 29.04 × age, so 4,515 is the effect at age 0, an age far outside the sample.

exam.explanation: Section 15.5 ('Don't'): the main-effect coefficient alone is conditional on age = 0. At the mean age (about 43) it is 4,515 + 29.04 × 43.3 ≈ $5,770.

exam.stem: In the same interaction model (age coefficient 127, interaction coefficient 29.04), what is the marginal effect of one more year of age for a worker with 16 years of education?

options.text: $127 per year of age
options.feedback: Revisit how the marginal effect of a regressor is computed when it is interacted with another (Key Concept 15.6).

options.text: $4,980 per year of age
options.feedback: Revisit how the marginal effect of a regressor is computed when it is interacted with another (Key Concept 15.6).

options.text: $465 per year of age
options.feedback: Revisit how the marginal effect of a regressor is computed when it is interacted with another (Key Concept 15.6).

options.text: $592 per year of age
options.feedback: Correct: ME<sub>age</sub> = 127 + 29.04 × 16 ≈ $592.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.6: in a model with age × education, the marginal effect of age depends on education: ME<sub>age</sub> = 127 + 29.04 × education = 127 + 464.6 ≈ $592 at 16 years of schooling.

exam.stem: Why does the naive prediction exp(predicted ln earnings) systematically underpredict earnings?

options.text: The average of exp(u) exceeds exp of the average of u, so exp(predicted ln y) misses a factor above 1.
options.feedback: Correct. By Jensen's inequality E[exp(u)] > exp(E[u]) = 1, so E[y|x] = exp(xβ) × E[exp(u)] exceeds exp(xβ).

options.text: The log model's R² is below 1, so its predictions fall short of actual earnings on average.
options.feedback: Revisit why exp(predicted ln y) is biased as a prediction of y (Key Concept 15.7).

options.text: The OLS coefficients of a log-linear model are biased estimates of the true coefficients.
options.feedback: Revisit why exp(predicted ln y) is biased as a prediction of y (Key Concept 15.7).

options.text: The residuals from a log-linear regression have a negative average.
options.feedback: Revisit why exp(predicted ln y) is biased as a prediction of y (Key Concept 15.7).

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.7: E[y|x] = exp(xβ) × E[exp(u)|x], and Jensen's inequality gives E[exp(u)] > exp(E[u]) = 1. Dropping that factor makes naive predictions too low even with good coefficient estimates.

exam.stem: The chapter's log-linear earnings model (ln earnings on age and education) has s<sub>e</sub> = 0.615. Assuming normal, homoskedastic errors, by what factor should each naive prediction exp(predicted ln earnings) be multiplied?

options.text: About 1.36
options.feedback: Revisit the normality-based correction factor in Section 15.6 and Key Concept 15.7.

options.text: About 1.21
options.feedback: Correct: exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2) = exp(0.615²/2) = exp(0.189) ≈ 1.21.

options.text: About 1.85
options.feedback: Revisit the normality-based correction factor in Section 15.6 and Key Concept 15.7.

options.text: About 1.46
options.feedback: Revisit the normality-based correction factor in Section 15.6 and Key Concept 15.7.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.7: the correction factor is exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2) = exp(0.615²/2) ≈ 1.21, so naive predictions are raised by about 21%. In the chapter this lifts the mean prediction from about $45,800 to about $55,400 (actual mean $56,369).

exam.stem: Duan's smearing estimator corrects retransformation bias without assuming that the errors are normally distributed.

options.text: True
options.feedback: Correct. Smearing multiplies by the average of exp(ûᵢ) across the residuals, so it does not rely on normality.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Revisit the alternative to the normality-based correction described in Key Concept 15.7.

exam.explanation: Key Concept 15.7: Duan's smearing estimator multiplies exp(predicted ln y) by (1/n)Σexp(ûᵢ), a nonparametric correction that lets the residuals themselves fix the bias. In the chapter's data it gives essentially the same correction as the normal-based factor.

exam.stem: Which statements about predicting earnings in dollars from the chapter's log-linear model are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The normality-based correction should use s<sub>e</sub> from the levels regression of earnings, not from the log regression.
options.feedback: Revisit the practical recommendations for predicting from log models (Section 15.6).

options.text: The correction matters more when the log regression's residual variance is larger.
options.feedback: Correct: the factor exp(s<sub>e</sub>²/2) grows with s<sub>e</sub>, so the bias is larger when the residual variance is larger.

options.text: The correction is needed only for workers whose predicted earnings exceed the sample mean.
options.feedback: Revisit the practical recommendations for predicting from log models (Section 15.6).

options.text: Comparing the mean of the corrected predictions with actual mean earnings is a useful check.
options.feedback: Correct: the chapter recommends checking whether predicted means match actual means.

options.text: Modeling E[earnings | x] directly, as a generalized linear model does, avoids the retransformation step.
options.feedback: Correct: the chapter lists GLMs as an alternative that needs no retransformation.

exam.explanation: Section 15.6: use s<sub>e</sub> from the log model, apply the correction to every prediction (not to the coefficients), expect larger bias when the residual variance is larger, check predicted against actual means, and consider smearing, the bootstrap, or GLMs as alternatives.

exam.explanation: Key Concepts 15.3 and 15.8: with ln(earnings) and a quadratic in age, the approximate percentage effect of one more year is 100 × (β<sub>age</sub> + 2β<sub>agesq</sub> × age) = 100 × (0.0561 − 0.0329) ≈ 2.3% at age 30; it shrinks with age and turns negative after about 51 years.

exam.stem: In the chapter's mixed log model, which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The self-employment coefficient (−0.118, p = 0.24) shows that self-employed workers earn significantly less than private-sector workers at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Revisit how each coefficient in the mixed model is interpreted and tested (Section 15.7).

options.text: The government coefficient compares government workers with private-sector workers who have the same gender, age, education, and hours.
options.feedback: Correct: private-sector workers are the omitted category for the two sector dummies.

options.text: Predicting earnings in dollars from this model calls for a retransformation correction, because its dependent variable is ln(earnings).
options.feedback: Correct: any prediction of earnings from a model for ln(earnings) needs the correction of Section 15.6.

options.text: The government coefficient (0.070, p = 0.13) is not statistically significant at the 5% level.
options.feedback: Correct: p = 0.13 is above 0.05.

exam.explanation: Section 15.7: the sector dummies compare self-employed and government workers with private-sector workers, holding the other regressors fixed; neither is significant at 5% (p ≈ 0.24 and 0.13). Because the dependent variable is ln(earnings), dollar predictions need the retransformation correction.
